designing-apis

更新
システムを設計する

ほかのコードから呼ばれるインターフェースを定義するときに使います——公開関数やライブラリのエントリポイント、HTTPやRPCのエンドポイント、IPCやワイヤ上のメッセージ、プラグインの契約、エクスポートされるモジュール境界。命名と粒度、必須引数と任意引数、デフォルト値、ページネーションと順序、enumの拡張、不透明なトークン、非推奨化と提供終了、バージョニング、そして提案された変更が破壊的かどうかの判断を扱います。

このページはまだ日本語に翻訳されていません——英語版を表示しています。

Overview

The interface is the only part you cannot refactor later: everything behind it is yours, everything in front belongs to callers you cannot deploy. Design the failure modes, the growth path, and the compatibility promise before the happy path.

When to use

  • Adding anything another team, process, or version will call: exported function, endpoint, message type, plugin hook, config key.
  • Deciding one call versus three; required versus optional; what to return for a collection.
  • Adding a field, parameter, enum member, or error code to something already shipped.
  • Someone asks "is this change breaking?"
  • Not for: choosing a single identifier's wording (naming-things), evolving stored data (schema-evolution), deciding where the boundary belongs at all (drawing-boundaries).

Shape and granularity

  • Write three call sites — the common one, the rare one, the awkward one — before the implementation. The common case must be reachable with the fewest arguments; the rare case must be reachable at all. If the awkward one requires reaching around the API, the shape is wrong.
  • One call per caller intent, not per stored entity. If every caller makes the same N calls in the same order, that sequence is the API and the N calls are leaked implementation.
  • Granularity follows call cost: in-process ≈ nanoseconds, IPC ≈ microseconds, network ≈ milliseconds. A boundary costing 1ms cannot expose per-field accessors; a boundary costing 10ns should not force a batch.
  • Name the effect, not the mechanism: cancel, not setStatusCancelled. Mechanism names age badly because the mechanism changes and the name cannot.
  • A boolean parameter is a design failure at the first one. render(true) is unreadable at the call site and the second flag creates a combinatorial mess. Use a named option type or enum from flag one.
  • Never let a field's meaning depend on another field's value. "If kind is A, payload is X" is a tagged union; ship it as a discriminated union with a closed shape.
  • One write path per provenance, not per row shape. Where a field encodes how strongly something is believed, writing an outside claim through the operation that means "we observed this" erases the distinction permanently — matching row shapes are what make the shortcut tempting, not what make it safe. tracking-data-provenance covers the claim taxonomy and the promotion rules that turn a laundered value into authority.

Required, optional, and absence

ConceptEncode as
Always meaningfulRequired field
Usually omitted, safe fallback existsOptional with a documented default
Meaningfully absentExplicit unset variant or sentinel, never a null shared with "not provided"
Patch semantics (unset vs cleared vs set)Three encodings, not two — a nullable field cannot express this

Optional-with-default beats nullable for two reasons: null forces every caller to branch, and on any wire format null is indistinguishable from "an older client did not send this field". Put the default in the contract so it is versionable; a default replicated into each caller silently drifts per client.

Designing for growth

  • Additive-only is the cheapest promise you can keep. Additive means: a new optional field, a new operation, a new enum member only if tolerance shipped first, a new error code only if callers were told to handle unknown codes by class.
  • Never return a bare closed enum you may need to grow. Every closed enum is a promise you will never add a member. If growth is plausible, ship an unknown/default arm and the client's obligation to tolerate it, wait a full deprecation window so tolerant clients are deployed, then add the member. Reversing that order is the standard way a client fleet crashes.
  • Opaque tokens — cursors, continuation handles, resume tokens, ETags — must be opaque in fact, not just in the docs: encode and sign or version the payload, and reject a token you did not mint. If callers can parse it, they will depend on it, and their dependency becomes your contract.
  • Reserve removed field names and tag numbers so a future field cannot reuse them and misparse old data.
  • An open extra: map<string,string> bag becomes a schema you never versioned and can never validate. Prefer a reserved namespace with an explicit no-compatibility statement, or nothing.

Collections, errors, idempotency

  • Any operation returning a collection needs, in v1: a limit with a documented default and maximum, a total ordering, and an opaque cursor. Retrofitting is breaking even behind a new version, because "returns all of them" is what callers built on.
  • Ordering must be total — tiebreak on a unique key. Ordering by a non-unique column under pagination silently duplicates and skips rows; this is the most common pagination bug and it never appears in small test data.
  • Enumerate the failures at design time; they are part of the type whether or not the language says so. Minimum: a stable machine-readable code, a retryable indicator, and an identifier the caller can quote back. See modeling-errors.
  • For every mutating operation, answer "the caller timed out and does not know the outcome" before shipping. If the answer is "they cannot tell", you designed a double-charge. See designing-for-idempotency.

Versioning and the compatibility contract

StrategyReal cost
No version, additive foreverCheapest to operate, strictest to design — nothing can ever be removed or renamed. Correct default.
Version in path or namespace (v2, libfoo2)You run N implementations, not N routes. Only viable with a published sunset date you actually enforce.
Per-request negotiation (headers, capability handshake)Fine granularity, combinatorial test matrix. Needs a flag per capability; a single increasing number degenerates to path versioning.
Per-field evolution (numbered schema fields)The only strategy that survives past a couple of versions. Requires never reusing a tag.

State three things explicitly: which surface is covered, how long an obsolete thing keeps working (in absolute time or releases), and how a break is signaled. Deprecation without a runtime signal is not deprecation — nobody reads changelogs; things that emit warnings get fixed. "Experimental" is only real when it is mechanically unpleasant to use (opt-in flag, unstable_ prefix); a documentation note does not stop anyone from depending on it.

Common mistakes

SymptomReal cause
Every new feature adds another boolean parameterOptions never modeled as a type; the first flag set the pattern
Every caller wraps the API in the same helperWrong granularity — their helper is the API you should have shipped
Adding an optional field broke old clientsContract never stated unknown-field tolerance, so parsers were strict
A new enum member crashed the fleetMember added before tolerant clients were deployed
"Page 2 and page 3 both contained item X"Non-total ordering under pagination
v2 quietly returns fewer results than v1Unbounded collection in v1; adding a limit is breaking regardless of the version label
Callers keep getting the call order wrongSequencing is a real constraint and belongs inside one call or an explicit state machine
Support asks callers to "check the error text"No stable error code in the contract
A caller broke when you changed a cursor's formatToken documented as opaque but never made opaque
An outside recommendation trips a threshold meant for first-party evidenceOne write path served two provenances, so the row records the value and forgets where it came from

Red flags

  • "We'll add pagination when it gets big."
  • "It's internal, we can change it later" — about something whose callers you do not deploy.
  • "Just return null for now."
  • "Callers shouldn't depend on that."
  • "We'll mark it experimental in the docs."
  • Adding a flag parameter instead of asking whether this is really two operations.
  • Reusing a write path because the row shape matches, without checking that the claim's provenance does.
次へ modeling-errors →

「システムを設計する」の他のスキル

  • modeling-errors 失敗をどう表現し、どう扱うか決めるときに使います——例外、ResultやEither型、エラーコード、パニック、スーパーバイザーのどれを取るか、catch・rescue・recoverのブロックを書くこと、エラー型やエラーの契約を設計すること、包むか、記録するか、投げ直すか…
  • designing-for-idempotency ある操作が2回以上届きうるときに使います——結果のわからないタイムアウトのあとのリトライ、at-least-onceのキュー、コンシューマの再起動と再配信、再生されたWebhook、ダブルクリックされたボタン、再開されたジョブ、書き込みの途中でのクラッシュ。
  • choosing-concurrency-model 同時に進めなければならない仕事があって、やり方が決まっていないときに使います——OSスレッド、非同期やイベントループ、アクターとメッセージパッシング、永続的なジョブキュー、データ並列、キーによるシャーディング。
  • modeling-state-machines 何かにライフサイクルがあるとき——注文、ジョブ、接続、アップロード、セッション、サブスクリプション、デバイス、ワークフローのステップ——あるいは複数の真偽値やフラグが1つのものを表しているときに使います。
  • drawing-boundaries 何を一緒にまとめるか決めるときに使います——モジュール、パッケージ、crate、ライブラリ、プロセス、サービスの分け方、コンポーネントの抽出や統合、ベンダーのSDKを自分の管理下にあるインターフェースで包むこと、フォルダ構成の組み直し。
  • caching-strategy キャッシュ、メモ化テーブル、CDNレイヤー、事前計算した読み取り経路を足すとき、保存したのに古いデータや誤ったデータが見えるとユーザーから報告があったとき、TTLやキャッシュキーを選ぶとき、ホットキーの期限切れやコールドスタートがオリジンを押し流すとき…
  • schema-evolution すでに本番で動いている契約を変えるときに使います——データベーススキーマ、シリアライズ形式、保存済みのドキュメント、APIのペイロード、キューのメッセージで、フィールドを追加・削除・改名・型変更すること。
  • data-migrations すでに存在するデータを、1つのトランザクションには収まらない規模でバックフィル・変換・再エンコード・移設するとき、使い捨てのスクリプトで数百万件のレコードを舐めなければならないとき、途中で殺されたマイグレーションを二重適用せずに再開しなければならないとき…
  • configuration-management 環境変数、設定、トグル、設定ファイルの項目を追加するとき、シークレットと設定が絡まっているとき、ステージングでは動くのに本番では動かないとき、欠けた設定や形の崩れた設定が起動から何時間も経ってnullやクラッシュとして表に出るとき、新しい環境やデプロイ先を立ち上げるとき…
  • instrumenting-for-observability 何をログに出し、何を計測し、何をトレースするか決めるとき、あるインシデントが手元のテレメトリでは説明できなかったとき、ラベルのカーディナリティでメトリクスやログの請求額が跳ねたとき、アラート・SLI・SLOを定義するとき…
  • rate-limiting-and-backpressure システムがさばける以上の負荷を受けているとき、スロットリング・クォータ・429レスポンスを設計するとき、キューが伸び続けたり何時間も遅れて捌けたりするとき、リトライが部分的な障害を全面的な停止に増幅するとき、コネクションプールやスレッドプールが枯渇したとき…
  • tracking-data-provenance Use when a record can be written from more than one kind of source — measured, imported, inferred, user-asserted…

La Boulangerie TBaguetteにはTBaguette’s Atelierが入っています——チケットとコミットのあいだにあって、判断で決めるしかないことがらを、きちんと片づいた作業台のように並べたところです。
